cards.front: What makes a freeway different from other roads?
cards.back: Freeways are multi-lane, controlled-access, divided highways with no stops and no cross traffic, built for long trips with less fatigue and more safety.

cards.front: What does safe freeway driving require, and where must slower vehicles drive?
cards.back: Safe freeway driving means keeping pace with traffic and staying alert, and vehicles moving slower than the normal flow must keep to the right.

cards.front: Why should you avoid weaving between freeway lanes?
cards.back: Weaving from lane to lane is dangerous; pick a lane moving at the pace you want and stay in it.

cards.front: What must you do before changing lanes to pass or exit?
cards.back: When you must change lanes to pass or exit, check traffic carefully and signal well before you move.

cards.front: What should you do if you break down on a freeway?
cards.back: In a freeway breakdown, park completely off the traveled lanes and stay with the vehicle if you possibly can.

cards.front: What distress signals tell officers you need help on a freeway?
cards.back: The distress signals are an open trunk, a raised hood if weather allows, and a white cloth tied to a door handle or antenna, and an officer who sees them will help.

cards.front: When may you park on a freeway?
cards.back: Parking on the freeway is not allowed except in an emergency.

cards.front: What are entrance ramps and acceleration lanes for?
cards.back: Entrance ramps are short one-way ramps that lead to an acceleration lane, where you speed up to match through traffic if possible.

cards.front: How do you merge from the acceleration lane?
cards.back: From the acceleration lane, watch for a gap, signal, and merge smoothly into traffic.

cards.front: Who yields when a driver enters the freeway?
cards.back: Freeway drivers should leave room for merging traffic, but an entering driver must yield if they do not.

cards.front: Should you stop in the acceleration lane?
cards.back: Do not stop completely in the acceleration lane unless it is absolutely necessary.

cards.front: What do you do at an entrance ramp with a YIELD sign and no acceleration lane?
cards.back: On an entrance ramp with a YIELD sign and no acceleration lane, entering drivers obey the sign and stop if needed instead of forcing their way in.

cards.front: What is an interchange?
cards.back: An interchange joins two highways at different levels with separate connecting roads, so vehicles can cross, enter or leave without interfering with others.

cards.front: What are the four common interchange types?
cards.back: Four common interchange types are directional, cloverleaf, diamond and trumpet.

cards.front: What does a directional interchange serve?
cards.back: A directional interchange serves heavy traffic moving between only two legs, with other movements handled by ordinary diamond-type ramps.

cards.front: What does a cloverleaf interchange use, and what does it remove?
cards.back: A cloverleaf interchange uses loop connections for turns on and off the freeway from four directions and removes left-turn and cross-traffic conflicts.

cards.front: How does a diamond interchange work?
cards.back: A diamond interchange has four ramps for entering or leaving with the flow, and left turns are made after you leave the freeway.

cards.front: When is a trumpet interchange used?
cards.back: A trumpet interchange gives freeway access where another road meets it in a T, as a variation of the directional or diamond design.

cards.front: Where do left turns happen at a diamond interchange?
cards.back: A diamond interchange lets you enter and leave with the flow on four ramps, and any left turn comes only after you are off the freeway, never on it.

cards.front: How should you prepare for a freeway exit?
cards.back: Plan your exit early and watch the signs, moving into the proper lane well ahead of time.

cards.front: Where should you slow down when exiting a freeway?
cards.back: To exit, signal, enter the deceleration lane and slow there, never slowing suddenly on the freeway itself, and be ready to yield or stop at the end of the ramp.

cards.front: What should you do if you miss your exit?
cards.back: If you miss your exit, do not stop, back up or turn around; go on to the next exit and come back.

decks.domain: Freeways and vehicle maintenance (equipment, maintenance, trip planning, confusables)

cards.front: What must a vehicle have to be driven safely?
cards.back: You cannot be a safe driver unless your vehicle is properly equipped and mechanically sound, and Alabama law sets the safety equipment required.

cards.front: What two brakes must every automobile have?
cards.back: Every automobile needs two separate ways of applying the brakes: a regular foot brake and a parking brake.

cards.front: What must a muffler do, and which devices are forbidden?
cards.back: Every vehicle needs a working muffler that stops excessive or unusual noise, and muffler cutouts, bypasses and similar devices are forbidden.

cards.front: What must the exhaust system not do?
cards.back: The exhaust system must not leak carbon monoxide into the vehicle and should be checked periodically.

cards.front: What must a vehicle with a windshield have?
cards.back: Any motor vehicle with a windshield must have wipers in good working order.

cards.front: How far behind must your rear view mirrors let you see?
cards.back: All vehicles must have rear view mirrors that let the driver see two hundred feet behind.

cards.front: Which lights must a motor vehicle have?
cards.back: Required lighting includes a minimum of two white headlights, one or more red taillights, a brake light, and a light over the rear license plate.

cards.front: How far must lights be visible, and how far must high beams reach?
cards.back: All lights must be visible from at least five hundred feet, and the high beam must light objects at least three hundred fifty feet away and stay properly aimed.
cards.memory_hook: five hundred seen, three fifty lit

cards.front: May you flash both turn signals to warn of a hazard?
cards.back: Flashing both turn signals, or another pair of lights, at the same time to warn of a vehicle hazard is permitted.

cards.front: How do the mirror, light visibility and high beam distances compare?
cards.back: Rear view mirrors must show two hundred feet behind, while every light must be visible from five hundred feet and high beams must reach three hundred fifty feet.

cards.front: How do safety belts help in crashes?
cards.back: In crashes, steering assemblies cause thirty percent of fatal injuries and hitting the windshield, its frame or the dash causes another forty percent, second collisions that safety belts can prevent.

cards.front: What do children under six need in a car?
cards.back: Children under six years old need special child and infant restraints to protect them from serious injury or death.

cards.front: Why do small children need restraints?
cards.back: Traffic crashes are the leading killer of children, and child and infant restraints keep small children from becoming flying missiles in a crash.

cards.front: Which vehicles may use bells, sirens or exhaust whistles?
cards.back: Every motor vehicle needs a working horn, and bells, sirens or exhaust whistles are allowed only on emergency vehicles.

cards.front: When may you use your horn?
cards.back: Use the horn only to give a warning reasonably needed for safety, never to announce arrival or call passengers, because needless use can lead to arrest.

cards.front: How should you care for your tires?
cards.back: Buy tires rated to carry your car's weight, check pressure often, never drive on under-inflated tires, and have uneven wear checked for wheel or alignment problems.

cards.front: When is a tire illegal?
cards.back: A tire is illegal once its tread is less than one or sixteen inch deep.

cards.front: How can you treat your tires kindly?
cards.back: Avoid jack-rabbit starts and screeching stops unless truly necessary, go easy on corners and rough roads, let tires cool on long hot trips, and check the spare now and then.

cards.front: May you use different types of tires?
cards.back: Never use different types of tires, and ask your dealer before mixing types between front and back.

decks.domain: Freeways and vehicle maintenance (equipment, maintenance, trip planning, confusables)

cards.front: Why does maintenance matter?
cards.back: Brakes, exhaust, cooling systems, lights, wipers and tires wear out, and any one left unmaintained could cause a serious crash, so have the car checked.

cards.front: How should you plan a freeway trip?
cards.back: Plan freeway trips with a map, deciding exactly where you will get on and off.

cards.front: What should you check before a freeway trip?
cards.back: Check fuel, water and oil before a freeway trip, because no service stations sit directly on freeways, and check every tire, including the spare.

cards.front: Where are most children hurt in pupil transportation?
cards.back: Most children hurt or killed in pupil transportation are outside the bus, struck by drivers who ignore its flashing red lights and stop arm, in the area called the DEATH ZONE.

recap_hooks.text: Keep right if slower, stay in your lane, and in a breakdown get fully off the road and show distress signals.
Use the acceleration lane to match speed, yield when entering, and know the directional, cloverleaf, diamond and trumpet interchanges.
Plan exits early, slow only in the deceleration lane, and go on to the next exit if you miss yours.
Cars need two brakes, a quiet muffler, working wipers, mirrors that see two hundred feet, and lights visible from five hundred feet.
Belts prevent second collisions, small children need special restraints, horns are only for warnings, and tires need enough tread.
Maintain worn parts, plan freeway trips with fuel and fluids checked, and stop for buses to protect the death zone.
